newsitem.title: USA: North American power grid braces for solar storm.
newsitem.headline: North American power grid braces for solar storm.

text.p: Power companies in the northern United States and Canada said Wednesday they were bracing for a solar storm that, if severe, could knock out their generating and transmission systems over the next few days.

"It has the potential to produce a severe impact on the power system ... and the potential to produce large area blackouts," said John Kappenman, supervisor of transmission power engineering at Minnesota Power in Duluth, Minn.
"But this is an immature science. Forecasting these phenomena is extremely frustrating, with only about a 30 percent accuracy range," he said.
"With 93 million miles of inter-planetary space to cross, that's a lot of uncertainty."

The call to action came from the National Aeronatics and Space Administration (NASA), which said Wednesday a large storm on the sun's surface probably would hit the earth's magnetic field later Wednesday and affect Earth through early Friday.

The solar storm was detected about 48 hours earlier by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, a WIND companion satellite that NASA and the European Space Agency launched in 1995 to keep a constant eye on the sun's surface.

A similar solar storm caused widespread disturbances on the North American power system on March 13, 1989, hitting Hydro Quebec especially hard, knocking out power across Quebec and nearly toppling the power grid in the U.S. Northeast.
Kappenman said nations close to the magnetic north pole are most exposed to such phenomena, called geomagnetic disturbances.

According to the North American Electricity Reliability Council (NERC), the areas most likely to see geomagnetic disturbances are the Pacific Northwest, the Rockies, the upper Midwest, eastern Canada and the East Coast as far south as Washington, D.C.

Gene Gorzelnik, director of communications at Princeton, N.J.-based NERC headquarters, said most power companies would likely pay extra close attention to ground currents at their units and perhaps trim loads on their systems, if necessary.
